blocks.content: The Directive Principles are like an instrument of instructions, which were issued to the Governor-General and to the Governors of the colonies of India by the British Government under the Government of India Act of 1935.

items: Unlike Fundamental Rights, DPSPs are non-justiciable and cannot be directly enforced in a court of law.
The concept of Directive Principles was borrowed from the Irish Constitution of 1937, which had copied it from the Spanish Constitution.
Courts can examine the constitutional validity of a law on the ground that it seeks to give effect to a Directive Principle.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: DPSPs denote the ideals that the State should keep in mind while formulating policies and enacting laws.
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the Directive Principles as 'novel features' of the Indian Constitution.
They embody the concept of a 'welfare state' aiming at social and economic democracy, rather than a 'police state'.
DPSPs are non-justiciable in nature, meaning they are not legally enforceable by courts for their violation.
Although non-justiciable, the Constitution itself declares that these principles are fundamental in the governance of the country.
